topic: Multi-intent task decomposition for LLM tool and skill routing
name: ToolLLM / ToolLLaMA
description: ToolLLM (arXiv:2307.16789, ICLR 2024 spotlight) is an open framework for instruction-tuning open-source LLMs (LLaMA) for real-world tool/API use. It contributes ToolBench (a ChatGPT-built instruction-tuning dataset over 16,464 RapidAPI APIs), ToolLLaMA (LLaMA fine-tuned on solution paths), a Sentence-BERT neural API retriever, and ToolEval. Its central methodological contribution is DFSDT (Depth-First Search-based Decision Tree), a search strategy that lets the LLM explore multiple reasoning/tool-call paths and backtrack, used both to annotate training solution paths and at inference. It is an early supervised approach to multi-tool routing.
decomposition_method: LLM-prompted reasoning, not an explicit decomposer. ToolLLaMA performs implicit step-by-step planning within a single agent loop rather than splitting the prompt into named sub-tasks. DFSDT (Depth-First Search Decision Tree) drives multi-step exploration: at each node the model emits a thought + API call, and the tree expands/backtracks across alternative reasoning paths. Training data (solution paths) is generated by prompting ChatGPT with DFSDT; ToolLLaMA is then SFT-trained on the successful paths. [uncertain]
decomposition_granularity: tool call. Each step in the DFSDT/ReACT trajectory is a single thought + one API (tool) call with arguments.
ordering_strategy: dynamic (mid-chain exploration with backtracking). DFSDT explores reasoning paths depth-first, can retract a step and try an alternative branch, then proceed along a promising path; order emerges from search rather than a fixed upfront plan or DAG.
decomposition_validation: No explicit decomposition-quality detector or reward model. Quality is enforced indirectly: during data construction only successful (passing) DFSDT paths are retained as SFT training data, so failed/invalid trajectories are filtered post-hoc rather than validated for solvability/completeness/non-redundancy before dispatch. At inference there is no separate verifier of the plan; the search itself (backtracking on dead ends) is the only correctness mechanism. [uncertain]
hierarchy_depth: flat. A single agent produces a linear (tree-searched) sequence of tool-call steps; there are no milestones, nested sub-agents, or skill-tree layers. The DFSDT 'tree' is a search structure over candidate next-steps, not a hierarchical task decomposition.
router_type: retrieve-then-(implicitly)-act, plus per-step selection. A dense API retriever first narrows the 16k+ API pool to a relevant candidate set for the instruction; ToolLLaMA then selects which retrieved API to call at each step inside the DFSDT loop. There is no standalone multi-label routing classifier.
routing_model: Two components: (1) a separate fine-tuned dense retriever (Sentence-BERT / BERT-BASE, trained with contrastive learning, positives = relevant APIs, sampled negatives) for API retrieval; (2) the prompted/fine-tuned ToolLLaMA itself for per-step API selection during reasoning. Baselines for retrieval were BM25 and OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002.
handles_ambiguity: best-effort pick via search. There is no clarification-request mechanism or abstention; ambiguity is resolved by DFSDT exploring multiple candidate paths and backtracking from unpromising ones, ultimately committing to a path that passes. No user-in-the-loop disambiguation. [uncertain]
fallback_behavior: retry via backtracking / 'give up' actions. When a branch fails or no productive API call is found, DFSDT retracts and explores another branch; the action space includes a finish/give-up action when no path succeeds within budget. There is no escalation to a human; failure is recorded as an unsolved instruction. [uncertain]
skill_pool_scale_and_retrieval: embedding retrieval (top-k) over a very large pool. ToolBench covers 16,464 real-world RESTful APIs across 49 RapidAPI categories; the Sentence-BERT API retriever embeds the instruction and each API document and ranks by cosine similarity to surface a top-k candidate set, making full-context infeasible. Retrieval quality measured by NDCG@1/@5; single-tool (I1) retrieval scores higher than multi-tool (I2/I3).
router_agent_asymmetry: Minimal/none. The retriever and the agent both effectively operate over the same API documentation (name + description + parameters); there is no deliberate design where the router sees richer skill text than the agent. The retriever is a separate model but not given privileged body-level information. [uncertain]
execution_pattern: sequential chain with tree search (DFSDT). One tool is called per step in a ReACT-style thought/action loop, augmented by depth-first backtracking across alternative branches; no parallel or concurrent tool execution.
parallel_vs_concurrent: Neither. Tool calls are issued one at a time within the reasoning loop; no parallel single-turn multi-call and no concurrent execution. [uncertain]
dependency_detection: assumed-sequential (implicit). Dependencies between tool calls are handled implicitly by the model's step-by-step reasoning (each step's output informs the next); there is no explicit dependency graph or independence classifier to enable parallelization.
result_aggregation: iterative then LLM-summarized. Each API response feeds the next reasoning step; once a viable path completes, the model composes a final answer from the accumulated observations. There is no typed structured merge. [uncertain]
mid_chain_feedback: hard (search-level re-planning). DFSDT explicitly re-plans: it can retract steps and switch branches based on intermediate API observations and failures, so later decisions react to earlier results rather than following a locked upfront plan.
benchmark_name: ToolEval (built on ToolBench), evaluated across instruction categories I1 (single-tool), I2 (intra-category multi-tool), and I3 (intra-collection multi-tool); plus instruction-retrieval evaluation via NDCG.
multi_intent_coverage: sequential / mixed multi-tool. Explicit multi-tool categories: I2 (multiple tools within a category) and I3 (multiple tools across a collection), in addition to single-tool I1. These are dependent multi-step compositions rather than independent parallel sub-tasks.
accuracy_metric: outcome + comparative. ToolEval uses Pass Rate (whether the instruction is completed within a budget) and Win Rate (ChatGPT-judged quality/efficiency of the solution path vs. ChatGPT-ReACT). Retrieval is scored by NDCG@1/@5. Reported: GPT-4(DFSDT) avg pass rate ~57.2; ChatGPT(ReACT) ~40.2; ToolLLaMA ~29 (numbers vary by version).
clarification_capability: Not supported / not measured. Neither ToolLLaMA nor ToolEval models a when-to-ask vs. when-to-answer decision; there is no clarification-question generation or measurement of clarification efficiency. The agent always attempts a best-effort solution. [uncertain]
process_vs_outcome_eval: primarily outcome-based (Pass Rate / Win Rate judge final solution completion and path quality), with DFSDT itself providing implicit process-level search but no explicit per-step process-reward scoring.
eval_stability: Live-API instability is a known limitation: RapidAPI APIs change/expire over time, so fixed ground-truth paths are infeasible and ChatGPT-as-judge is used instead. This instability later motivated StableToolBench's cached/virtual API server; original ToolEval numbers are less reproducible across time. [uncertain]
integration_pattern: standalone framework/pipeline: a fine-tuned retriever feeds candidate APIs into an in-context prompted agent (ToolLLaMA) running a DFSDT loop, executing against the RapidAPI tool server. Not a LangGraph/middleware/inference-engine integration.
routing_layer: application-layer. Retrieval and tool selection occur in the model/application stack; no inference-engine-layer routing. [uncertain]
latency_overhead: Notable: DFSDT's tree search expands and backtracks across multiple branches, issuing many more LLM calls and API calls than a single ReACT pass, trading higher latency/token cost for higher success on hard (I2/I3) instructions. The retrieval step adds one dense-retrieval pass before the loop. [uncertain]
online_adaptation: static. The retriever and ToolLLaMA are trained offline (SFT on DFSDT-annotated paths); there is no production-feedback bandit/RL loop or continual online fine-tuning in the original work.
adoption: open-source (with code, Apache 2.0): OpenBMB/ToolBench repo provides dataset, ToolLLaMA models, retriever, and ToolEval. Widely used as a research baseline/dataset; ICLR 2024 spotlight. Not a commercial product.
